conclusion.justification: The report concludes that honey probably helps reduce acute cough symptoms in children over one year old, describing it as a reasonable symptomatic option while noting that benefits are modest and evidence certainty is limited.
conclusion.label: leans_endorse

report:
**Conclusion: yes—probably, but the benefit is modest and the evidence is limited.** For children **over 1 year** with an acute cough (typically from an upper-respiratory infection), honey appears to improve parent-reported cough frequency/severity and sleep compared with no treatment, placebo, or diphenhydramine. NICE summarizes reductions of roughly **0.5–2 points on a 7-point carer-reported scale at one day**.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng120/chapter/summary-of-the-evidence

The 2018 Cochrane review found honey probably reduced cough frequency versus no treatment/placebo (mean difference **−1.05** points; 95% CI −1.48 to −0.62; **2 studies, 154 children**).  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007094.pub5/full

However, the trials were small, outcomes were subjective and short-term (often one night), and evidence certainty is low. A newer systematic review therefore concluded that honey *may* outperform cough medicines or placebo/no treatment for symptoms and sleep, but called for better blinded placebo-controlled trials.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37355498/

So, honey is a reasonable symptomatic option—not a cure or evidence of treatment for the underlying illness—and should not delay medical assessment for breathing difficulty, dehydration, or persistent/worsening illness.

**Critical safety limit:** never give honey to a child **under 12 months**, because it can cause infant botulism.  
https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/foods-and-drinks/foods-and-drinks-to-avoid-or-limit.html
